C1.justification: v1 centers its contribution on learnability-based SFT selection and balancing conversational and mathematical capabilities. v2 additionally claims a normalized RHO generalization linked to implicit rewards, effectiveness across LLaMA and Gemma, broad superiority over selection methods, and an approximately 8% relative improvement from DavIR-DPO. These substantially expand the claimed contribution and applicability.

C2.justification: v2 develops a sequential-context explanation for length bias and interprets backbone-mismatch results as evidence of model-dependent learnability. Its limitations now identify failed GSM8K compression, with competing explanations involving reasoning capabilities and cross-entropy's suitability. It also explains that learnability selection does not ensure quality or diversity. These replace much of v1's future-work discussion about generation, augmentation and mixture proportions.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the single human annotator's characteristics and comparison instructions, greedy decoding, and reuse of the published AlpaGasus subset rather than fresh ChatGPT scoring. These are limited disclosures, not demonstrated changes to the earlier experiments. Some earlier details, including the explicit GPT-4 judging temperature of zero, are no longer stated; comprehensive training hyperparameters remain absent.

E1.justification: v2 adds human-curated LIMA data for subset training, UltraFeedback preference pairs for the new alignment task, and MBPP data for length-correlation diagnostics. It also evaluates new experiments on the AlpacaEval benchmark described in Appendix E. These extend the represented data and task coverage beyond v1's Alpaca selection, mixed instruction evaluation and GSM8K mixing.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated EL2N, forgetting-score and DataInf comparators in Table 6, vanilla DPO in Table 8, and multiple DPO variants in the length-correlation comparison of Table 3. The latter are diagnostic comparisons, not end-to-end performance evaluations. RHO-LM corresponds to v1's existing unnormalized loss-difference variant; full-data, random and ChatGPT-selection comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: Added protocols include Gemma-2B subset-size comparisons, controls that mismatch selection and retraining backbones, and Zephyr-7B-SFT preference training with ordinary and length-controlled AlpacaEval metrics. Table 6 evaluates Gemma against GPT-4, distinct from the earlier Text-Davinci-003 comparisons. These are substantial new experimental designs, without establishing that retained LLaMA experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands length-bias diagnostics across datasets, models and DPO objectives (Tables 1–3), tests model dependence through backbone mismatches (Table 7), and investigates failed GSM8K compression (Figure 5). It adds selected-example cases in Table 11. Earlier normalization and category analyses remain, while v1's loss-versus-ranking scatterplots are removed.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without confidence intervals or significance tests. v2 Appendix E introduces 1,000 bootstrap samples from the 805-question AlpacaEval dataset, 95% confidence intervals in Table 12 and t-test p-values in Table 13. These quantify evaluation-question resampling, not repeated training runs or additional seeds.

E6.justification: The original LLaMA curves and appendix overlap/category counts are largely retained, but substantial new results appear. Table 6 reports Gemma win rates of 20.2 for DavIR with 6,000 examples versus 18.3 for full-data training. New Table 8 reports length-controlled win rates of 61.83 for DavIR-DPO versus 57.23 for vanilla DPO. LIMA compression, correlation, model-mismatch and GSM8K failure results are also added.

M1.justification: The normalized SFT selection formula and full-data reference-model procedure are retained despite renaming. However, v2 introduces DavIR-DPO, a new preference-training objective that normalizes preferred and rejected responses' log-probability ratios by their reference-model losses (Section 3.2, Equation 4). This substantially extends the method beyond selecting SFT data.

P1.justification: Beyond the LoBaSS-to-DavIR rename and author-information changes, the abstract, introduction and method narrative are extensively rewritten around RHO, length dependence and implicit rewards. Experiments are reorganized into SFT and DPO sections with new thematic subsections, conclusion and limitations change order, and the appendix is reorganized into Sections A–E.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column to a two-column layout, with substantially redrawn and relabeled performance plots. The workflow diagram is removed and algorithm pseudocode is added; the loss-ranking scatterplots disappear. Numerous new comparison and statistical tables and a GSM8K failure plot are introduced, while existing appendix tables and sunburst charts are relocated and reformatted.

R1.justification: v2 repositions the method as a normalized adaptation of RHO connected to DPO, rather than principally introducing a novel learnability criterion. Related work expands substantially into implicit rewards, preference-optimization variants and classical coreset selection, including RETRIEVE, CRAIG, EL2N and influence methods. This changes both the cited literature and the account of the work's novelty.

T1.justification: v2 adds a formal connection between loss-reduction scoring and the Bradley–Terry/DPO implicit-reward representation (Section 3.1, Equation 2), then defines a normalized preference-learning objective in Equation 4. This extends the mathematical formulation beyond SFT subset scoring. The denominator-invariance proof itself is retained from v1 Appendix A.2 as Proposition 1 in v2 Appendix C.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1's narrow comparative validation through additional selection baselines, an independent model family, backbone-mismatch controls and an explicit GSM8K failure analysis. These help establish where the method works and qualify its applicability. The gains are tempered by overclaims: Table 6 contradicts consistent superiority over full-data training, and t-tests on bootstrap replicates provide weaker significance evidence than claimed. Nevertheless, the added controlled comparisons, clearer research positioning and concrete limitations substantially improve the paper's overall evidential value.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same model-dependent data-selection work, renamed from LoBaSS to DavIR. The normalized SFT score, original experiments, proof and appendix analyses can be matched across versions. The complete main texts, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds Gemma comparisons, length-correlation measurements, model-mismatch experiments, GSM8K compression tests and Zephyr preference-training results.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLaMA-7B/13B fine-tuning experiments, GPT-4 and human evaluations, Alpaca/GSM8K mixing results, and analyses of selected examples.

results.title: DavIR: Data Selection via Implicit Reward for Large Language Models

C1.justification: V1 principally claims successful autonomous GitHub tool extension and learning from human experience. V2 makes OpenAct a central benchmark contribution, claims a gap in existing open-domain evaluation, and adds claims of superiority over baselines and experimental validation of hierarchy and bi-level experience learning.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of the ablations, hint dependence, application difficulty, and failures from unnecessary tool use. Its new limitations section identifies GitHub-specific applicability, reproducibility problems from changing repositories, and Docker resource demands. Earlier repository-selection and configuration failure explanations are largely retained.

D1.justification: V2 adds benchmark construction and validation procedures, repository/domain/difficulty inventories, Apply and Judge prompts, CPU and base-image disclosures, and a stated code/data release link. Conversely, v1's complete query list and several specialized prompts, including Issues/PR judgment and experience summarization, are no longer supplied in the PDF.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from four repositories in four domains to OpenAct's 21 repositories across seven domains, retaining the original four while adding network analysis, security analysis, visualization, and additional specialized tasks. V2 also systematically evaluates explicit, implicit, and absent repository hints: 113 base queries produce 339 variants.

E2.justification: V1 evaluates only GitAgent. V2 Table 3 adds actual comparisons against vanilla LLMs, ReAct, and ReAct+Summary using GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, plus GPT-4-based XAgent. ReAct receives the same available actions as OpenAgent.

E3.justification: OpenAgent's settings change from gpt-4-32k at temperature 0.6 to gpt-4-0125-preview and gpt-3.5-turbo-16k at 0.7, with an explicit zero-shot setting. V2 replaces phase-level success checking with GPT-4-judged answer matching and a completeness rubric, and introduces a 120-case judging validation and a 51-query experience-reuse experiment.

E4.justification: V2 adds Issues/PR removal and cross-task experience ablations, controlled repository-hint comparisons, setup/application difficulty analyses, and human-versus-GPT-4 judging validation. V1's stored-repository retrieval-accuracy and API/token-cost analyses disappear. Most execution case studies are retained, chiefly in Appendix E.

E5.justification: V1 Section 3.1 specifies five runs per query and says averages and standard deviations are reported, although Table 2 displays only point values. V2 omits repeated-run counts and provides no variability estimates. This changes statistical documentation without establishing that the actual number of runs decreased.

E6.justification: V1's four-repository phase results and 69.4% headline success rate are replaced by extensive new benchmark results. V2 Table 3 reports OpenAgent averages of 47.3% for GPT-4 and 17.1% for GPT-3.5; Table 4 reports 40.3% without Issues/PRs. These are results under changed tasks and settings, not directly comparable performance changes from v1.

M1.justification: Hierarchical decomposition, Issues/PR consultation, and stored environments and experience already exist in v1; their renamed presentation does not establish new components. A concrete procedural refinement appears in the setup prompt: v1 Figure 16 forbids creating a Dockerfile, whereas v2 Appendix A.3 permits creating one when the default base image causes errors.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and method narrative are extensively rewritten, and GitAgent becomes OpenAgent. Related work moves earlier, benchmark construction precedes the method, detailed procedures and case studies move into appendices, and dedicated limitations and evaluation-validation sections are added.

P2.justification: The document changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column layout. V2 adds benchmark-positioning, construction, performance, and judging-agreement graphics and reorganizes tables around domains, baselines, and ablations. Original case-study diagrams are largely relocated or reformatted, while the cost plot and query-list figures disappear.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning around domain-knowledge, tool-use, repository-level, and open-ended benchmarks. Section 2 and Table 1 introduce comparisons with works including ScienceQA, SciEval, SWE-Bench, ML-Bench, and SUPER, reframing the contribution as a benchmark and agent system rather than primarily a tool-extension method.

T1.justification: V2 recasts v1's descriptive action-observation and hierarchical-decomposition equations in recursive agent notation. This does not introduce a substantive mathematical result or change the underlying formal relationships. Neither version supplies theorems, proofs, or mathematical guarantees.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical coverage and absence of baseline comparisons and component ablations. Broader task coverage, comparisons with matched available actions, experience-learning tests, and human checks of automated judging strengthen the evidence for effectiveness. These gains outweigh omitted run-count/cost information and the inconsistency between Section 3.4's completeness rubric and Appendix A.6's judging instructions, which still weaken reproducibility.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same GitHub tool-integration research, with GitAgent renamed OpenAgent and substantial retained procedures and examples. All 22 pages of v1 and 21 pages of v2, including appendices, support comparison despite extensive revision.

after.justification: V2 reports original OpenAct evaluations, baseline comparisons, experience-learning ablations, difficulty analyses, and human validation of automated judging.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments on 30 queries across four repositories, including phase success rates, stored-repository retrieval accuracy, API/token costs, and execution case studies.

results.title: Enhancing Open-Domain Task-Solving Capability of LLMs via Autonomous Tool Integration from GitHub

C1.justification: The central claim of detoxification while preserving general utility remains. v3 gives prototype-based learning and hard negatives greater prominence and adds the abstract's claim that these pairs ensure robust, stable optimization. This strengthens a methodological claim while retaining the principal application and contribution.

C2.justification: v3 Sections 7–8 add substantive limitations concerning generator and corpus coverage, residual toxicity, adversarial bypasses, English-only evaluation, and demographic bias. Section 5.3 newly interprets positive-only training as encouraging input repetition and negative-only training as producing degenerate outputs. These considerably expand the account of mechanisms and applicability boundaries.

D1.justification: v3 adds a source-code link, NVIDIA A10G hardware, approximately 1.5-hour Mistral training time, an estimated 2,500 GPU-hour experimentation budget, LoRA target layers in Table 9, and the judge prompt in Appendix A.3/Figure 5. These substantially expand reproducibility information. LoRA rank and scaling are retained, while v1's exact all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embedding-checkpoint identification is omitted.

E1.justification: v3 adds WikiText2 for open-domain fluency evaluation in Section 5.4. SafeNLP detoxification, white-box and black-box tasks, and the ten downstream utility benchmarks are retained. The demographic breakdown analyzes populations already represented in SafeNLP.

E2.justification: v3 Table 1 adds reported comparisons with CHRT using GPT-2 and Mistral-7b, Model Arithmetic, and additional GPT-2 variants. Table 4 adds PPO, DPO, and SimPO comparisons using Mistral-7b. These substantially expand comparison methods beyond v1's principal comparisons with underlying language models; DPO's earlier citation alone was not an evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: The reported negative-weight settings change from β in {0, 0.5, 3.5} to direct α in {1, 1.1}. New protocols include dist-n diversity metrics, perplexity evaluation on held-out sets with 0/50/75/100% toxicity, and Qwen-2.5-7b judging with randomized candidate order. The existing generation settings and downstream benchmark shot counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 Section 5.3 adds positive-only and negative-only loss ablations and tests one versus seven samples per contrastive set. Section 5.4 adds fluency, diversity, and toxicity-mixture analyses; Appendix A.2 adds results for 13 demographic groups. The earlier embedding visualization and qualitative examples are retained, with the embedding analysis moved into the main text.

E5.justification: v1 provides point estimates without a repeated-run count. v3 Section 4.1 first specifies five fine-tunings with different random seeds and adds extensive ± reporting in experimental tables. The meaning of ± is not defined. This establishes substantially changed uncertainty reporting, without establishing an increase from a known earlier run count.

E6.justification: Reported CP toxicity values change, including Falcon-7b from 30.6% to 36.6% and Mistral-7b from 4.7% to 4.3% in Table 1. Black-box and instruction-tuned results also change, and v3 adds comparator, ablation, fluency, diversity, judge-preference, and demographic results. Changed method specifications and run reporting prevent treating these revisions as controlled same-setting gains or losses. v1 Table 4's downstream utility values are unchanged in v3 Table 6.

M1.justification: The stated training objective changes materially: v1 Section 2.2 uses exp(|ϕ(x)−c|/τ), whereas v3 Section 3.2 uses exp(−|ϕ(x)−c|)/τ. This reverses the distance preference and changes temperature dependence. Prototype averaging and the paraphrase-generation procedure remain. The PDFs establish a changed method specification but do not resolve which implementation produced each result.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition, and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting, including a new communication metaphor and expanded prototype-based explanations. The document gains dedicated related-work, limitations, and ethics sections; results are reorganized, and the embedding analysis moves from the appendix into the main text.

P2.justification: v3 redraws Figure 1 and expands experimental tables with additional comparators and uncertainty columns. It adds ablation, perplexity, demographic, and LoRA tables plus judge-preference and prompt figures. The instruction-tuning comparison is incorporated into a diversity table, while the algorithm and resized embedding visualization move into the main text. The utility table and qualitative examples are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds an extensive Previous work section covering controlled decoding, preference optimization, knowledge editing, paraphrasing, and hard-negative learning. It develops explicit distinctions from approaches including CMD, GPT-Detox, Model Arithmetic, and LongLLMLingua, with numerous additional citations. v1's explicit identification of the loss as an InfoNCE variant and its corresponding citation are removed.

T1.justification: The mathematical definition of the central contrastive score is substantively revised through the exponential sign and temperature placement. These formulas are non-equivalent. In v3 Equations 3–4, the common 1/τ factor cancels from the normalized score, contradicting the accompanying explanation that it affects learning dynamics. Neither version supplies theorems or proofs resolving these issues.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's limited competitive comparisons, absent component ablations, and missing run-variability reporting. The ablations expose degenerate low-toxicity solutions, while generation-quality checks, demographic results, explicit limitations, and implementation details make the claims more assessable. Important weaknesses remain: the revised temperature cancels mathematically, Algorithm 1 retains an objective-sign inconsistency, and ± values are undefined. Nevertheless, the added empirical scrutiny and transparency provide a substantial net improvement over v1.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Contrastive Perplexity research. Their main text and appendices are readable, and visual inspection resolves extraction issues in equations, figures, and tables. The substantial revision supports a reliable comparison.

after.justification: v3 reports original detoxification results, comparator experiments, component ablations, generation-quality evaluations, and demographic analyses, alongside retained results.

before.justification: v1 reports original detoxification experiments, downstream utility measurements, embedding analysis, and qualitative outputs in the main text and appendix.

results.title: Contrastive Perplexity for Controlled Generation: An Application in Detoxifying Large Language Models

C1.justification: The introduction extends headline findings to few-shot evaluation and distinguishes GPT weaknesses in concatenation/intersection from open-model weaknesses in union. The central contributions—automatic KG-based CAQA construction and its usefulness for assessing and training attribution evaluators—remain unchanged.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations involving keyword co-occurrence, CoT decomposition errors and annotators' missing domain knowledge. It also discusses fact-level evaluation failures and explicitly limits coverage of lengthy answers, mathematical, temporal, spatial and domain-specific reasoning. V1 offers much narrower interpretation and limitations.

D1.justification: V2 adds code/data access information, licensing, annotation guidelines and filtering procedures, few-shot/CoT/FACTSCORES prompts, and the ALCE augmentation recipe. It documents vLLM, revised inference hardware and the 3,000-example GPT evaluation limit. However, v1's explicit GPT snapshot identifiers are omitted.

E1.justification: V2 augments whole-answer attribution classification with atomic-fact support estimation and explicit KG-to-text fidelity assessment. The underlying sources remain GrailQA/WebQuestionsSP over Freebase and ALCE; ALCE-FineGrained expands the earlier ALCE-derived evaluation without introducing a new domain.

E2.justification: Tables 5, 15 and 16 substantially expand evaluated comparators with LLaMA-3/3.1, Gemma-2, Phi-3, Qwen-2.5, GPT-4o variants and CoT evaluators. The ALCE comparison adds CAQA-trained T5-11B and further-adapted Vicuna. V1's separate LLaMA-2-chat rows are absent from v2's full results.

E3.justification: V2 introduces few-shot protocols, FACTSCORES evaluation and adaptation using 800 GPT-4-labeled/edited ALCE examples. Four-category ALCE annotations increase from 50 to 215, and AutoIS comparisons now merge negative labels into a binary category. The main-text CAQA human-check count changes from 600 to 300, while Appendix H describes larger annotation pools. Table 4 also revises complexity-group counts while retaining the total dataset size.

E4.justification: New analyses include a 100-example generated-text audit, fact-level evaluation of 200 partially supportive cases, sensitivity to demonstration count, CoT comparisons, domain adaptation and an attribution-error analysis of 234 Vicuna-generated examples. The earlier complexity analysis and ALCE case studies are retained or reorganized.

E5.justification: V2 adds inter-annotator reliability reporting: Fleiss' kappa of 0.780 and 0.748 in Appendix H, and Cohen's kappa of 0.758 for the text audit. V1's automatic-versus-human kappa of 0.65 is no longer reported, while Pearson correlation remains 0.97. Model scores still lack repeated-run uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive few-shot, CoT, fact-level and adaptation results, including CAQA versus human FACTSCORES of 0.62 versus 0.58. Existing entries also change: zero-shot Vicuna-13B overall F1 is 0.143 in v1 Table 5 and 0.405 in v2 Table 16, whereas several fine-tuned rows remain identical. These are revised reported results, not established same-setting performance gains.

M1.justification: The core generator retains query extension, subgraph editing and ChatGPT verbalization. Appendix E.3 adds an auxiliary CoT evaluator that decomposes answers into atomic facts, classifies each fact and aggregates the classifications into an attribution label.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and evaluation narrative are extensively rewritten. Benchmark construction is reorganized into four subsections, appendices expand from A–D to A–I, and the narrative and results rename insufficient as partially supportive. The title and author information also change.

P2.justification: V2 replaces the opening illustration with a construction-pipeline figure and a category-example table, combines category and complexity results into broader tables, and adds several experimental tables and annotation-guideline figures. Complexity examples move to Appendix Table 17, while the earlier ALCE case study reappears as Table 18.

R1.justification: V2 adds AttributionBench, discussion of unanswerable-question attribution, and relevant newer model and evaluation literature. Table 1 separates AttrEval-Gen from AttrEval-Sim, and the positioning explicitly acknowledges extrapolatory/irrelevant equivalence. These refine the comparison with prior work while preserving the original research framing.

T1.justification: Table 3 corrects the formal path-extension expression: the added edge now connects to the original head e0, rather than v1's inconsistent e1 reference. The underlying logical operators and intended query structures remain stable, and neither version introduces theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation through generated-text audits, fact-level human comparisons and a fairer AutoIS comparison using matched binary labels and T5 architecture. Diagnostic experiments, annotation guidelines and access information address important weaknesses in v1's validation and reproducibility. Unexplained complexity-count revisions and omitted GPT snapshot identifiers remain drawbacks, but the net quality gains are substantial.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CAQA research and provide readable main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices. Renaming, relocation and substantial expansion do not prevent reliable comparison.

after.justification: V2 reports original model evaluations, fact-level attribution results, human validation studies and supplementary experiments (Tables 5–8 and Appendices A, E–H).

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluator experiments on CAQA and ALCE-Manual, plus comparisons with human annotations (Tables 5–7 and Section 6).

results.title: Can LLMs Evaluate Complex Attribution in QA? Automatic Benchmarking using Knowledge Graphs

C1.justification: V2's abstract, introduction and conclusion elevate scalar initialization and motif/phrase-aware whole-song composition into central contributions. V1 primarily emphasized symbolic tuples, token efficiency and dataset construction. The revised claims explicitly emphasize structural coherence and repetition while retaining unified generation and superiority over GPT-4.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations connecting initialization to embedding geometry, motif repetition to a diversity tradeoff, and phrase tokens to structural attention. It discusses memorization evidence and adds substantive limitations concerning dependence on singing synthesis, vocal expressiveness and missing accompaniment generation.

D1.justification: V2 documents the 5,120-token limit, All-In-One phrase annotation, text-to-song prompt construction, revised formats and detailed human-evaluation procedures and participant characteristics. Conversely, FL Studio is replaced by an unspecified internal transcription model, while v1's pitch-augmentation, token-budget and evaluation-calibration details are no longer provided.

E1.justification: The reported paired training corpus changes substantially: v1 combines LMD-full, Reddit, OpenCpop, M4Singer and scraped Mandarin songs; v2 describes 8K Chinese/English pairs collected from audio sources, including newly collected English pairs. V2 also explicitly evaluates pure-melody continuation. Both languages and the four headline tasks remain.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 removes the Transformer Baseline and Baichuan 2, replaces Qwen with Qwen 1.5, and adds InternLM 2 and a fine-tuned InternLM 2 control. The melody-to-lyric comparison also gains SongMass and LLaMA 2, which were absent from v1 Table 3.

E3.justification: Validation changes from 1,188 songs, comprising 415 Chinese and 773 English songs, to 100 split equally between languages. Training batch size changes from 8 to 1, and whole-song training replaces the described short-segment approach. V2 introduces repetition metric RR and continuation-based ablation protocols, substantially revising experimental settings.

E4.justification: V2 adds phrase-token and initialization ablations, a motif-repetition threshold sweep, alignment-granularity comparisons, attention/PCA analyses, memorization testing and annotated song case studies. The pretraining-dataset ablation is retained in Appendix D.3 with revised results; v1's duration/note-vocabulary ablation is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports random seeds, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or statistical significance tests. V2's additional experiments continue the point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Objective, subjective and ablation results are extensively revised, and structural and memorization findings are added. SongComposer's continuation MD/BERT score changes from 2.56/0.683 in v1 Table 4 to 2.12/0.662 in v2 Table 3, which adds RR of 1.64. These are results under revised settings, not established same-setting improvements. Separate English/Chinese lyric-to-melody scores disappear.

M1.justification: V1's logarithmic duration discretization and 120-note vocabulary are replaced by beat-based durations, a restricted 36-pitch vocabulary and revised tuples. V2 adds scalar pitch initialization, motif-level training and phrase tokens, and changes the backbone from InternLM-7B to InternLM2-7B (Sections 3.1-3.3 and 4.2).

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction and related work are extensively rewritten. Dataset construction moves largely into Appendix A, detailed subjective criteria move into Appendix B, and method, experiments and appendices are reorganized. The title, author list and dataset terminology also change.

P2.justification: V2 merges the objective conversion-task tables, removes language-separated columns and redesigns the continuation table. It removes the two-stage training schematic and adds hierarchical-structure, attention, memorization, embedding and annotated-score figures. Retained diagrams and prompt templates are also relocated or reformatted.

R1.justification: Related work shifts from contrasting SongComposer with acoustic music generation toward positioning it among symbolic composition subtasks and symbolic LLMs. V2 acknowledges ChatMusician and ComposerX and expands task-specific literature, while removing discussions of works including M2UGen, Noise2music and Mousai.

T1.justification: Mathematical changes concern specific constructions: v1's logarithmic duration encoder/decoder equations are replaced by clipped, tempo-dependent beat quantization. V2 also specifies scalar pitch-embedding multipliers and defines RR as total melodic lines divided by unique lines. Neither version develops theorems or proofs.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens empirical support for its design choices: the fine-tuned-backbone control and direct alignment, initialization and structural ablations address questions left largely untested by v1's dataset/vocabulary studies. Human-evaluation documentation and explicit limitations also improve transparency. The smaller validation set, loss of language-specific results and unspecified internal transcriber weaken evaluation breadth and reproducibility, but the controlled analyses provide a substantially stronger methodological justification overall.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SongComposer and retain its symbolic lyric-melody composition framework and four main tasks. Their main texts, appendices, equations, tables and figures support reliable comparison despite substantial revisions.

after.justification: V2 reports objective and human-evaluation results, component ablations, attention and embedding analyses, memorization testing, and generated-song case studies.

before.justification: V1 reports original objective comparisons, a 30-participant human evaluation, and dataset and vocabulary ablations in Tables 1-6.

results.title: SongComposer: A Large Language Model for Lyric and Melody Generation in Song Composition

C1.justification: The central claim that modern translation models are more robust remains. However, the mitigation contribution is substantially redefined: v1 emphasizes diminishing correction benefits for stronger models, whereas v2 claims that finetuning or correction lets conventional models exceed GPT-3.5 on three of four noise types, and that correction combined with LLMs surpasses it across the synthetic benchmarks.

C2.justification: V2 attributes robustness more strongly to training data following the OPUSLLM control and reverses v1's interpretation that correction and inherent robustness are not complementary. It adds explanations of deletion difficulty and mitigation data efficiency, plus explicit limitations concerning possible test contamination, high-resource languages, restricted natural-noise domains and exclusively automatic evaluation.

D1.justification: V2 supplies OPUSLLM training settings, detailed mitigation-data construction, revised training/decoding libraries and metric identifiers, and changes the stated code-repository location. Conversely, earlier batch-size, GPU and training-limit disclosures and several explicit checkpoint paths disappear. Keyboard layouts, prompts and MultiLexNorm statistics largely move to appendices rather than becoming new disclosures.

E1.justification: FLORES, MTNT and MultiLexNorm retain their language and domain coverage. Correction training changes from NeuSpell PROB+WORD to synthetically corrupted Tatoeba Challenge text, and the main synthetic mitigation evaluation shifts from English–French to English–Portuguese. These are limited coverage changes within the existing translation and correction tasks.

E2.justification: V2 adds OPUSLLM as an architectural comparator and synthetic-noise-finetuned OPUS as a mitigation comparator. It removes MTNT-finetuned NLLB and excludes GPT-3.5 from the MTNT correction comparison. JamSpell remains in intrinsic correction results but disappears from downstream translation comparisons, while ByT5 replaces mT5. TOWER/TI and finetuned OPUS/r/OPUS are matched across renaming.

E3.justification: The main TowerInstruct evaluation changes from 7B to 13B parameters. V2 introduces matched mitigation training with 60% corrupted source tokens, mixed clean/noisy validation and 100k/1m/5m training budgets. For retained MTNT OPUS finetuning, validation changes from every 100 to 500 steps and the learning-rate grid expands. Appendix H adds BLEU and chrF evaluations.

E4.justification: V2 adds the OPUSLLM architecture control, mitigation training-size analysis, synthetic sentence-level benefit/harm analysis and tests of synthetic finetuning on MTNT. V1's GPT-2 perplexity analysis of fluency versus adequacy is removed. The model-size/multilinguality and tokenizer analyses are retained, rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. Regression slopes remain point estimates without uncertainty reporting; additional scores and language averages do not introduce a new uncertainty-estimation practice.

E6.justification: Numerous benchmark entries and rankings change, and substantial result sets are added or removed. For example, MTNT English–French changes from Tower-7B scoring 80.65 below GPT-3.5's 81.33 in v1 Table 8 to TI-13B scoring 81.91 above the unchanged GPT-3.5 score in v2 Table 7; this involves a changed model setting. V2 also adds architecture, mitigation, training-size and BLEU/chrF results.

M1.justification: Section 5 replaces the mT5-Large source corrector with ByT5-Small and introduces direct OPUS finetuning on synthetically corrupted translation data. These change the mitigation architecture and training procedures substantially. The underlying perturbation types and COMET-slope approach remain unchanged despite terminology changes.

P1.justification: Beyond local wording and terminology edits, Section 5 is reorganized from source correction into a comparative mitigation narrative. V2 condenses substantial main-text explanations, redistributes technical material into Appendices A–H and adds a dedicated limitations section. This is a substantial structural revision despite the nearly unchanged abstract.

P2.justification: V2 restructures FLORES tables into translation-direction groups with averages, adds a TI-13B curve to Figure 1 and introduces new mitigation tables and plots. V1's fluency scatterplot, correction grid and MTNT correction scatterplots disappear. Several retained tables move to appendices, which also add six BLEU/chrF result tables.

results.title: HelpSteer3: Human-Annotated Feedback and Edit Data to Empower Inference-Time Scaling in Open-Ended General-Domain Tasks

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list and conclusion retain the same benchmark contribution and main claims: retrieval helps provenance, larger models better classify relationships, closed-source models generally lead, and relationship classification remains difficult. Revised scores do not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: The new error discussion attributes mistakes to relationship confusion, rare Other cases and possible overinterpretation caused by retrieved context. Appendix B.1 explains the differing confusion-matrix sample sets. Existing limitations concerning absent hallucination cases and context-window constraints remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v3 adds a dataset-access link in the abstract, detailed human annotation guidelines in Figure 10, and disclosure of matrix filtering and pass@5 in Appendix B.1. Existing model specifications, retrieval parameters and LLM annotation/evaluation prompts are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same LongBench, LooGLE and CRUD-RAG subsets covering 11 scenarios, English and Chinese, and single-, multi- and long-document settings. Tables 1 and 4 retain the same dataset composition.

E2.justification: Tables 3, 6 and 7 retain the same LLMs and retrieval comparators. However, v1 Figure 5 labels a plotted series qwen25_14b, whereas v3 Figures 5–6 label it Qwen1.5-14b while Section 5.4 still discusses Qwen2.5-14B. The PDFs do not resolve comparator replacement versus a legend error.

E3.justification: The new confusion-matrix analysis introduces an explicitly filtered evaluation: untraced sources are excluded, producing different DP and RA sample sets (Appendix B.1). Existing context-window handling, retrieval settings and the 13-metric framework remain. The added pass@5 statement is a disclosure, without evidence establishing a switch in the earlier experiments' protocol.

E4.justification: v3 adds GPT-4o DP/RA confusion matrices and relationship-level error analysis in Section 5.4 and Figure 7, examining quotation/compression/inference confusions and rare Other cases. Existing retrieval comparisons and scenario/source-length analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix B.1 newly reports pass@5 for all assessments, adding information about evaluation across multiple attempts. Sampling and estimation details remain unspecified, and an increase in runs is not established. Annotation-agreement reporting is unchanged; neither version supplies confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Relationship and overall F1 scores change throughout Tables 3, 6 and 7. GPT-4o RA macro relationship F1 changes from 63.09 to 36.94 and overall F1 from 62.02 to 48.97, with corresponding precision/recall unchanged. Qwen1.5-7B also has revised precision/recall results. In single-document English RA, Table 7's leader changes from Kimi (61.39 versus Gemini's 59.71) to Gemini (48.39 versus Kimi's 45.42). New confusion counts are also reported.

M1.justification: The three-stage annotation pipeline, BM25/Dense/LCS top-10 retrieval, DP/RA tracing procedures and prompts are retained. v3 standardizes the annotator name to GPT-4o, already identified in v1's Figure 2 and Appendix C. The added human guidelines document the existing procedure.

P1.justification: Most prose and section ordering remain intact. Local edits standardize GPT-4o terminology, expand inference examples and update experimental commentary. v3 adds Appendix B.1 and acknowledgements and shortens the prompts heading, without a broad narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v1's compact four-panel Figure 5 is redrawn and substantially enlarged into separate scenario and source-length figures in v3. New displays include the two confusion matrices and human annotation handbook. Existing prompt figures are retained as Figures 8–9, while numerical result tables preserve essentially the same structure.

R1.justification: The bibliography and substantive related-work discussion are unchanged. TROVE retains the same positioning relative to citation generation, fact verification and grounded generation.

T1.justification: Section 3's formal task definition, Equation 1's retrieval aggregation and Section 5.2's evaluation definitions are retained. Neither version introduces theoretical propositions or proofs. Expanded relationship examples and annotation instructions do not revise the mathematics.

improvement.justification: v3 repairs widespread internal inconsistencies in the central benchmark results: v1 reports GPT-4o RA relationship F1 of 63.09 despite precision/recall of 42.68/32.87; v3 reports 36.94 and revises corresponding results throughout Tables 3, 6 and 7. This substantially improves the quantitative evidence's credibility. Clearer plots, annotation instructions and dataset-access information add value. Underspecified pass@5, conflicting Qwen legends and Appendix B's mislabeling of the 42.99 GPT-4o RA score as DP remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh the central corrections.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TROVE benchmark and evaluation framework. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, including v3's added human annotation guidelines.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark evaluations and annotation-agreement results and adds GPT-4o confusion matrices in Figure 7.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 11 LLMs in Tables 3, 6 and 7, alongside dataset statistics and annotation-agreement results.

results.title: TROVE: A Challenge for Fine-Grained Text Provenance via Source Sentence Tracing and Relationship Classification

C1.justification: The central benchmark contribution and value-priority findings remain. The stated evaluation scope expands to 44 LLMs, and the conclusion adds an explicit warning that demographic-persona synthetic data generation risks inducing or amplifying downstream demographic biases.

C2.justification: Section 6 and new Appendix L substantively qualify cultural generalization, annotator diversity, and treating self-reported PVQ scores as ground truth. Additional discussion interprets cross-loadings, explains weaknesses of targeted response generation, and qualifies scaling trends with small-model exceptions.

D1.justification: Appendix C adds source-specific filtering criteria, intermediate counts, value-diversity thresholds, and the final allocation of 26 queries per source. Footnote 1 changes a promised future release to stated code/data repository availability. Appendix G.1 supplies additional model identifiers and broadens the reported evaluation period to February-April 2025.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 104 queries and 520 query-response pairs from ShareGPT, LMSYS, Scruples/Reddit, and Dear Abby, alongside PVQ-21, BFI-10, and ESS demographic assessments. UltraChat supplies a taxonomy for analyzing existing queries, not additional evaluation data.

E2.justification: New Table 2 directly compares Value Portrait's value-distribution balance with ValueNet and ValueFULCRA. These competitors already appeared in Appendix B's annotation-agreement investigation, but their participation in this distribution comparison is new.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from 27 to 44 model configurations, adding Claude/Gemini reasoning comparisons and size series for Qwen2.5, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen, and Gemma3. New analyses introduce GPT-o3-mini topic classification, distribution-balance metrics, and circular-distance comparisons. Existing temperature-zero and six-prompt evaluation settings remain.

E4.justification: Section 3.3 adds topic and value-coverage diagnostics; Appendix C.2 tests whether multiple value correlations follow Schwartz's circular structure. Appendix D adds a qualitative comparison of response-generation approaches, while Appendix G.4 extends reasoning and scaling analyses across model families and identifies small-model exceptions.

E5.justification: Prompt averaging, correlation-significance thresholds, power information, and Cronbach-alpha reporting are retained. No new repeated-run, seed, confidence-interval, or significance-testing practice appears. The added standard-deviation and variance columns describe dispersion across value dimensions, not uncertainty across runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1-3 and 7-8 add substantial results, including cross-loading distances averaging 1.59 versus 3.54 and 17 additional model profiles. Table 7 reports Benevolence scores of 0.65 and 0.95 for Claude-3.7-Sonnet and its thinking variant. All original numerical result tables retain their values after renumbering.

M1.justification: The five-response generation approach, human-rating correlations, item selection, Likert assessment, and score normalization remain unchanged. New Appendix C expands documentation of query filtering without establishing that the construction procedure changed.

P1.justification: The title, affiliation and acknowledgment text, several explanations, and conclusion/limitations are revised. Coverage analysis and new appendix sections are inserted with corresponding renumbering. Most existing prose and the overall narrative order remain intact.

P2.justification: v2 adds five tables and enlarges Figure 3. The original eight-panel demographic Figure 5 becomes four larger figures: age remains in the main text, while gender, politics, and education move to the appendix as Figures 6-8. These demographic plots redisplay retained results.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for UltraChat, PVQ-21, BFI-10, and newly evaluated model families. The related-work organization and central positioning against perceived-value annotation methods remain substantially unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix C.2 newly defines circular distance between value dimensions and same-direction versus opposite-direction correlation pairs using the positive and negative 0.3 thresholds. This provides a limited mathematical specification for the new analysis; the existing Cronbach-alpha formula remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's evidential foundation and reproducibility. Coverage and cross-loading analyses address previously unexamined aspects of representativeness and construct validity; additional model-family comparisons test the breadth of the original findings. Detailed filtering documentation and explicit cultural and self-report limitations make the work easier to assess and interpret. These gains are substantial despite the retained method and remaining limits on generalization.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Value Portrait study. Their complete text, tables, figures, and appendices support comparison, with retained content identifiable despite the changed title and renumbering.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds evaluations of 17 models, dataset-coverage analyses, and an analysis of correlations with multiple value dimensions.

before.justification: v1 reports original human-survey correlations, evaluations of 27 LLMs, and demographic-persona and value-steering experiments.
